opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me.

When we started Cosmos, we were trying to solve a very practical problem. People building physical AI, like robots and autonomous vehicles, need a lot of data, and real-world data is expensive, slow to collect, and sometimes dangerous to collect. So the first idea was: can we build a model that understands how the world evolves well enough to generate realistic futures? Then developers could post-train it for their own setting and use it as a data engine or a simulator.

In the early versions, we approached this as a family of models. We had models focused on prediction, generating what happens next from text, images, or video. We had models focused on transfer, taking structured inputs like segmentation, depth, or simulation renders and making them photorealistic. Then we had reasoning models that look at a video and answer questions about it, like whether this is physically plausible, or what the robot should do next. Each piece was useful, and releasing them separately let the community adopt the parts they needed.

But as we worked with more users, we kept seeing the same thing. These capabilities aren't really separate. To predict the future well, you need to reason about physics, intent, and cause and effect. To reason well about a scene, it helps a lot to be able to imagine how it might unfold. And control signals, whether text, actions, or geometry, are just different ways of conditioning the same underlying understanding of the world. Keeping them in separate models meant duplicating learning, and the gaps between them became a bottleneck. You'd generate with one model, check it with another, and convert formats in between.

So the lesson was that the world is one thing, and the model should represent it as one thing. Understanding and generation should share the same internal representation, so improvements in one transfer to the other. That's the philosophy behind moving toward a single world model: one system that can take in many modalities, reason about what's going on, and generate what comes next, including actions, and that you can post-train once for your robot or your car instead of stitching a pipeline together.

There was also a scaling argument. In language, we saw that one general model trained on a lot of diverse data beat many specialized models. We believed physical AI would follow a similar path, and our experiments increasingly supported it. Unifying lets us pour all our data and compute into one model and get compounding returns.

It wasn't easy. Balancing objectives, making generation quality and reasoning quality improve together, and making it efficient enough to be useful took a lot of iteration. But looking back, the earlier versions were how we learned what each component needed, and that's what made unification possible.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss how offering many Cosmos models can make it harder for users to choose one.

r006.rationale: The response does not say that maintaining multiple released models spreads development resources thin or slows iteration.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When we started Cosmos, we didn't set out to build one model. We set out to solve a problem, which is that physical AI, robots, autonomous vehicles, anything that has to act in the real world, is starved for data. You can't collect enough real-world experience to cover every situation a robot will encounter, and you certainly can't afford to let it fail in the real world while it learns. So the first Cosmos was really a toolbox. We had diffusion models, we had autoregressive models, we had tokenizers, we had separate pieces for generation, for prediction, for reasoning about what's happening in a scene. Each piece was built to answer one question well.

What we learned from putting that toolbox in front of developers was humbling. Every team used it differently, and the seams between the components became the bottleneck. You'd generate a scene with one model, try to predict the future with another, ask a third to judge whether the outcome was physically plausible, and the hand-offs lost information at every step. Developers didn't want to orchestrate five models. They wanted to describe a situation, ask what happens next, and trust the answer.

The deeper lesson was about physics itself. A model that only generates pretty video learns the look of the world. A model that only predicts the next frame from action inputs learns the dynamics but not the semantics. We kept seeing that when we trained these jointly, each capability made the other better. The generation got more physically consistent because the model had to be predictive, and the prediction got more general because the model had seen the enormous diversity of visual data. That was the signal that we were fighting our own architecture by keeping them separate.

Cosmos 3 is the result of taking that seriously. One model that understands, simulates, and generates, with a shared representation of the world underneath it. It can take in video, text, actions, and sensor data, and it can produce the same kinds of outputs, so the robot's policy, the simulator, and the evaluator are all looking at the same internal picture. There's also an efficiency argument. Training one large foundation model and specializing it is far cheaper than maintaining a family of models that drift apart over time.

I'd say the path was less about a grand vision and more about listening to where the friction was. The friction was always at the boundaries between models, so we removed the boundaries.

r003.rationale: It mentions a shared representation of the world, but does not say that the model learns it through compression.

r004.rationale: It says joint training improved generation and prediction, but does not describe combining reasoning, prediction, transfer, and policy data to raise a unified model’s performance ceiling.

astra-6.text:
Working on Cosmos pushed me toward a question: what should be shared across all these different tasks? Predicting what happens next, understanding a scene, and reasoning about the consequences of an action all require some understanding of the same underlying world.

If we build those capabilities separately, we risk learning that understanding repeatedly, in ways that don’t necessarily agree. That’s the motivation for moving toward a single world model in Cosmos 3: a shared foundation that can support different tasks while keeping its understanding of the world consistent.

And by “single,” I don’t mean that every application should behave identically. A robot may need a different interface from a system generating video. The idea is that underneath those interfaces, the model should connect what it sees, how the world changes, and how actions affect that change.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that the world is not divided into separate tasks. Understanding what is happening, predicting what happens next, and understanding how an action changes the outcome are all closely connected. They depend on the same underlying understanding of the physical world.

That motivates the move toward a single world model in Cosmos 3: a shared foundation that can support those different capabilities. But “single” doesn’t necessarily mean one model doing everything equally well. The important thing is that the capabilities share a coherent understanding of the world, so what the model perceives, predicts, and uses to reason about actions stays consistent.
